One-shot pruning and low-rank decompositions for LLMs. Post-training one-shot compression is a training-free paradigm popularized by SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) , which compresses a pretrained LLM layer-by-layer on a small calibration set by minimizing the layerwise reconstruction error ‖ 𝐗𝐖 − 𝐗 ​ 𝐖 ^ ‖ F 2 \|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2} subject to a structural constraint on 𝐖 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{W}} ; methods differ along two axes: the constraint family and the per-layer solver. Pure sparsity : SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) uses a sequential column-based sparsification scheme: after sparsifying one column, the remaining weights are updated to compensate for the incurred error, while ALPS ( Meng et al., 2024 ) formulates the same problem as a constrained quadratic problem solved by the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) ( Boyd et al., 2011 ) . Pure low-rank : SVD-LLM(W) ( Wang et al., 2025 ) uses a whitened Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to minimize layerwise reconstruction error; ASVD ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) instead scales input channels using activation statistics before SVD. Sparse + low-rank ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) : OATS ( Zhang and Papyan, 2025 ) and Hassle-free ( Makni et al., 2025 ) alternate a sparse fitting step with a low-rank projection step; OATS scores weights using a per-row activation-norm criterion whereas Hassle-free uses the full input correlation matrix. 3BASiL ( Makni et al., 2026 ) runs a multi-block ADMM that jointly minimizes the sparse and low-rank components simultaneously. Our method CACTUS differs from all these layerwise reconstruction algorithms by incorporating downstream gradients in its objective, making it curvature-aware rather than gradient-blind .

In this paper, we first highlight the connection between downstream utility and influence preservation through the curvature-aware objective introduced in Equation 1 . Our new algorithm CACTUS makes optimizing this objective practical for modern LLM pruning as well as ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) decomposition tasks. It runs at a substantially lower cost compared to prior state-of-the-art curvature-aware pruning methods. Across various compression settings, model architectures, and gradient projection strategies, CACTUS consistently improves downstream utility while retaining gradient fidelity. Limitations. In this paper, we focus on pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) compression. Extending our ADMM framework to quantization and mixed quantization-sparsity settings are directions for future work, especially when reparameterizations (e.g., rotations) change gradient geometry. We also only consider uniform compression budgets; it would be interesting to design specialized methods that can allocate sparsity and rank non-uniformly across the entire LLM layers. Additionally, we do not study post-compression refinements like full-model or LoRA-style finetuning. These may trade off deployment quality and gradient alignment fidelity in different ways. We leave these interesting follow-up research directions for future work.

All one-shot baselines are run in the same layerwise compression framework and with the same calibration samples, except when a method explicitly includes a post-compression stage. SparseGPT , ALPS , SVD-LLM(W) (simple activation-aware low-rank fitting without sequential factor refinement or post-compression fine-tuning), OATS , and 3BASiL use activation-only objectives using 𝐇 \mathbf{H} , whereas IPSVD , IProX , LLM-Surgeon , and CACTUS use 𝐆 \mathbf{G} as well. We also employ the five-shot setting described in Section 3.1 , since the one-shot unstructured pruning on Llama3.2-1B produced weak results. One-shot pruning and low-rank decompositions for LLMs. Post-training one-shot compression is a training-free paradigm popularized by SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) , which compresses a pretrained LLM layer-by-layer on a small calibration set by minimizing the layerwise reconstruction error ‖ 𝐗𝐖 − 𝐗 ​ 𝐖 ^ ‖ F 2 \|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2} subject to a structural constraint on 𝐖 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{W}} ; methods differ along two axes: the constraint family and the per-layer solver. Pure sparsity : SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) uses a sequential column-based sparsification scheme: after sparsifying one column, the remaining weights are updated to compensate for the incurred error, while ALPS ( Meng et al., 2024 ) formulates the same problem as a constrained quadratic problem solved by the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) ( Boyd et al., 2011 ) . Pure low-rank : SVD-LLM(W) ( Wang et al., 2025 ) uses a whitened Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to minimize layerwise reconstruction error; ASVD ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) instead scales input channels using activation statistics before SVD. Sparse + low-rank ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) : OATS ( Zhang and Papyan, 2025 ) and Hassle-free ( Makni et al., 2025 ) alternate a sparse fitting step with a low-rank projection step; OATS scores weights using a per-row activation-norm criterion whereas Hassle-free uses the full input correlation matrix. 3BASiL ( Makni et al., 2026 ) runs a multi-block ADMM that jointly minimizes the sparse and low-rank components simultaneously. Our method CACTUS differs from all these layerwise reconstruction algorithms by incorporating downstream gradients in its objective, making it curvature-aware rather than gradient-blind .

ultaneously. Our method CACTUS differs from all these layerwise reconstruction algorithms by incorporating downstream gradients in its objective, making it curvature-aware rather than gradient-blind . This is best illustrated in Figure 1 .

In this paper, we first highlight the connection between downstream utility and influence preservation through the curvature-aware objective introduced in Equation 1 . Our new algorithm CACTUS makes optimizing this objective practical for modern LLM pruning as well as ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) decomposition tasks. It runs at a substantially lower cost compared to prior state-of-the-art curvature-aware pruning methods. Across various compression settings, model architectures, and gradient projection strategies, CACTUS consistently improves downstream utility while retaining gradient fidelity. Limitations. In this paper, we focus on pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) compression. Extending our ADMM framework to quantization and mixed quantization-sparsity settings are directions for future work, especially when reparameterizations (e.g., rotations) change gradient geometry. We also only consider uniform compression budgets; it would be interesting to design specialized methods that can allocate sparsity and rank non-uniformly across the entire LLM layers. Additionally, we do not study post-compression refinements like full-model or LoRA-style finetuning. These may trade off deployment quality and gradient alignment fidelity in different ways. We leave these interesting follow-up research directions for future work.

2610.22794:1be6366f42989c1fa9f4d7b8f8809.question: In the 1B LLaMA pretraining experiments, what are Ori's validation-loss or perplexity results, peak training memory, and training throughput versus GaLore, other low-rank optimizers, and full-rank baselines at matched rank, model, data, and token budget?

passages.text: We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

passages.section: E.8 Measuring optimizer state peak memory
passages.text: Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . Python code for profiling optimizer peak memory. ⬇ import torch # Model and optimizer setup model = … optimizer = … # Main training loop for batch in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Forward and backward pass loss = model (** batch ). loss loss . backward () # Record the current memory usage after model backward mem_after_backward = torch . cuda . memory_allocated () # Reset the max memory counter torch . cuda . reset_peak_memory_stats () # Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Read the optimizer-incurred max memory # The difference with mem_after_backward is the # maximum additional memory caused by optimizer.step() peak_mem_during_step = torch . cuda . max_memory_allocated () optim_peak_mem = peak_mem_during_step - mem_after_backward

We profile the optimizer state peak memory and wall-clock time during the pre-training experiments from Section 5.2 . Details on the memory profiling procedure can be found in Section E.8 . As shown in Table 9 , Ori exhibits a superior efficiency profile among standard, non-error-feedback gradient-subspace methods (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). In addition, as shown in Table 10 , O-LDAdam demonstrates competitive and comparable efficiency profile to the error-feedback baseline LDAdam under the large update frequency regime ( T = 200 T=200 ). Full table on pre-training of other model sizes can be found in Appendix F . Memory Usage: Compared to standard, non-error-feedback baselines, Ori consistently consumes the least optimizer peak memory across all ranks. For instance, at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB). This confirms Ori’s tangible memory savings. On the other hand, compared to the error-feedback methods, O-LDAdam consistently yields the same memory footprint as LDAdam baselines. Training Speed: Despite updating its subspace projector 10x more frequently ( T Ori = 20 T_{\text{Ori}}=20 vs. T GaLore/OSD = 200 T_{\text{GaLore/OSD}}=200 ), Ori is still the fastest among all standard, non-error-feedback methods. While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

On the other hand, although O-LDAdam yields a slightly longer average update time than LDAdam with T = 200 T=200 due to the need to perform power iterations multiple times ( Algorithm 3 ), the additional cost is not prohibitively large. Moreover, O-LDAdam demonstrates a nontrivial speedup compared to the standard LDAdam setting with a per-step update schedule ( T = 1 T=1 ). Together with the model performance results shown in Table 2 , this demonstrates that O-LDAdam strikes a good balance between model performance and computational cost in the extremely low-rank regime. Table 11 presents the full results of memory and Wallclock time comparison of all the optimizer methods on the LLaMA model pre-training task on the C4 dataset. As shown by the table, our method Ori achieves superior memory and computation time profile almost across the broad, demonstrating its general efficiency under various settings. 2610.23571:c9d24bcc5bc6616812d95f4882c29.question: What measured post-training channel-pruning accuracy or perplexity does BMuon achieve versus Muon and other pruning-aware baselines at matched model, training compute, and retained width? Does it evaluate language models, and what are the unpruned-quality costs?

passages.text: Muon has demonstrated strong training efficiency across model scales, from small vision and language-model benchmarks to billion-parameter language models ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) . Its matrix update can be viewed as a linear minimization oracle over a spectral-norm ball, giving Muon a steepest-descent interpretation in spectral-norm geometry ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) . Prior work has shown that implicit bias can depend on optimization geometry ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) . For Muon, recent theory identifies a spectral-norm margin bias in linear and smooth homogeneous models ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Gronich and Vardi, 2026 ) . Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers degrade rapidly under structured MLP pruning, suggesting that Muon’s spectral geometry does not by itself encourage structured compressibility. As shown in Figure 1 , a Muon-trained ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K collapses after only 30 % 30\% global MLP channel pruning, with Top-1 accuracy falling from 75.23 % 75.23\% to 3.17 % 3.17\% . In contrast, our proposed Budget Muon (BMuon) algorithm retains 74.08 % 74.08\% Top-1 accuracy after 70 % 70\% pruning, nearly matching its 74.17 % 74.17\% accuracy before pruning, with no post-pruning recovery. This raises the central question: can Muon’s spectral geometry be modified to encourage structured compressibility?

Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , where α \alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and K K is the global budget over the N N hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

2610.23343:f62307d9d5164e0513536318c4a7a.question: What assumptions are required for the bottleneck-rank bounds and the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay? Does the paper test these predictions in language-model fine-tuning against standard LoRA or full fine-tuning, and with what measured results?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

Our answer starts with a simple observation: once the backbone is frozen, the loss does not observe an adapted matrix T T directly, but only through a finite-rank linear map determined by the frozen activations. Concretely, if H = [ h 1 , … , h N ] H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}] is the matrix of frozen input features across the N N training samples, the empirical loss depends on T T only through the product T ​ H TH . We call rank ⁡ ( Φ ) \rank(\Phi) , where Φ ⁡ ( T ) = T ​ H \Phi(T)=TH , the bottleneck rank of the adapted block. The same principle applies blockwise to multiple adapted stages and attention heads. Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output. This yields exact low-rank existence results without linearizing the network around the pretrained weights. For multi-head attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , the same principle becomes sharper because attention introduces additional invariances: row-wise softmax is unchanged by additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and the frozen output projection. Table 1: Comparison with the closest related theoretical analyses of LoRA. This work Jang et al. (2024) Kim et al. (2025) Requires NTK linearization No Yes No Multilayer multi-head attention bound Yes (Thm. 4.4 ) No No Spurious local minima excluded No (Prop. 4.9 ) Yes (NTK) Partial Additional loss assumptions Differentiability and stagewise C 1 C^{1} regularity NTK-regime conditions Restricted strong convexity and smoothness Generalization bounds Yes Yes No Our contribution is summarized as follows.

• Low-rank representer theorem for trace-norm fine-tuning. For a frozen network in which an adapted block T T is observed only through a finite-rank linear map Φ ⁡ ( T ) \Phi(T) of bottleneck rank d Φ d_{\Phi} , we prove that the trace-norm-regularized problem has a global minimizer whose rank is controlled by d Φ d_{\Phi} ; see Theorem 4.1 . The multi-stage extension is Theorem 4.3 . • Rank bounds from attention invariances. For multi-head attention, query and key updates are observable only through centered score subspaces because row-wise softmax is invariant to row-wise additive constants. Value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. Combining these invariances with projector compression gives the optimizer-dependent subspace rank bounds in Theorem 4.4 . • Generic first-order rank deficiency for factorized LoRA. For the weight-decayed LoRA factorization, we prove that after a generic positive semidefinite perturbation, full-column-rank first-order stationary points are excluded whenever the Pataki–Barvinok rank threshold exceeds the dimension of the associated family of symmetric KKT matrices; see Theorem 4.7 . The multistage and attention consequence are Theorem C.9 and Corollary 4.8 . This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation. • Perturbation transfer and generalization. We show that global minimizers of the perturbed factorized objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm-regularized problem when the perturbation is small; see Theorem 4.10 .

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

Our answer starts with a simple observation: once the backbone is frozen, the loss does not observe an adapted matrix T T directly, but only through a finite-rank linear map determined by the frozen activations. Concretely, if H = [ h 1 , … , h N ] H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}] is the matrix of frozen input features across the N N training samples, the empirical loss depends on T T only through the product T ​ H TH . We call rank ⁡ ( Φ ) \rank(\Phi) , where Φ ⁡ ( T ) = T ​ H \Phi(T)=TH , the bottleneck rank of the adapted block. The same principle applies blockwise to multiple adapted stages and attention heads. Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output. This yields exact low-rank existence results without linearizing the network around the pretrained weights. For multi-head attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , the same principle becomes sharper because attention introduces additional invariances: row-wise softmax is unchanged by additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and the frozen output projection. passages.text: Monarch–Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining Alexander Miasnikov 1 , Kabirov Ruslan 1 , Gleb Molodtsov 1 , Dmitrii Vlashchuk 1 , Vladimir Aletov 1 , Nail Bashirov 1 , Daniil Tikhonov 1,2 , Maxim Krutikov 1 , Aleksandr Shestakov 1,3,* , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1 1 BRAIn Lab 2 HSE University 3 MBZUAI * Work performed at BRAIn Lab prior to joining MBZUAI. Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. 2610.17730:912f71b6e1c7f26b131d71beb95ab.question: In language-model fine-tuning, what task-level results does DT-LoRA achieve versus standard LoRA, other rank-adaptive LoRA variants, and full fine-tuning at matched rank, trainable parameters, and training budget? What memory or runtime overhead does randomized SVD add?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA .

To address this challenge, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch that accumulates task-specific directions as in standard LoRA and a dynamic branch that periodically absorbs principal residual directions outside the current tangent space. We prove that, under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints, the optimal update for a local quadratic model is given by the truncated SVD of the tangent-space residual gradient. Crucially, this residual inherits a factored structure from backpropagation, enabling its products with narrow matrices to be computed directly from cached input activations and output gradients. This structure allows us to construct matrix-free operators for Matrix-Free Randomized SVD, which extracts the principal residual directions via randomized SVD [ 7 ] without explicitly forming the residual gradient. To incorporate these directions while maintaining training stability, we introduce Controlled Write-back mechanism, which merges them with the current dynamic branch update, compresses the result back to the original rank, and bounds the relative change at each refresh. After training, both branches are merged into the pre-trained weights, yielding the same inference cost as standard LoRA.

We evaluate DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks: the 19 image classification tasks in VTAB-1K; object detection and instance segmentation on MS COCO; open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation (OVDG-SS) in both real-to-real and synthetic-to-real settings; eight commonsense reasoning tasks using LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B; and GLUE using DeBERTaV3-base. Under matched trainable parameter budgets, DT-LoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and its variants. On MS COCO, DT-LoRA at r = 16 r=16 achieves an average score of 46.6, exceeding LoRA at the same rank by 8.2 points and outperforming LieRA [ 29 ] , which uses twice as many trainable parameters. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA establishes new state-of-the-art results, surpassing the task-specific S 2 -Corr [ 46 ] despite being a general-purpose fine-tuning method. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify a geometric limitation of factorized LoRA: substantial gradient energy lies outside the current tangent space. Across ten representative LoRA variants, we show that this tangent-space residual exhibits strong spectral concentration, and establish that its truncated SVD yields the optimal update under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints for a local quadratic model. • We propose DT-LoRA, which partitions a fixed rank budget into Stable and Dynamic branches to incorporate principal residual directions. Matrix-Free Randomized SVD extracts these directions without materializing the residual gradient, while Controlled Write-back integrates them with accumulated updates and bounds the change at each refresh, enabling dynamic tangent-space adaptation without additional trainable parameters or inference overhead.

• We demonstrate the effectiveness of DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks, with consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants under matched trainable parameter budgets. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific methods and establishes new state-of-the-art results.

On GLUE ( Tab. 6 ), DT-LoRA achieves the highest average score of 88.7, outperforming LoRA under the same parameter budget by 1.1 points and AdaLoRA, which uses more trainable parameters, by 0.6 points. It also surpasses full fine-tuning (88.3) while training less than 1% of the model parameters. The largest improvement over LoRA is observed on QQP, with a gain of 3.6 points.

As shown in Tab. 8 , DT-LoRA matches LoRA’s trainable parameter count while introducing modest training overhead. With τ = 5 \tau=5 , it requires 0.89 0.89 s per iteration, only 70 70 ms more than LoRA, and is 5.11 × 5.11\times faster than explicitly forming the residual gradient and applying full SVD ( 4.55 4.55 s per iteration). The four configurations isolate the contributions of randomized SVD and matrix-free computation. Randomized SVD restricts the decomposition to an ℓ \ell -dimensional sketch and accounts for most of the measured runtime reduction; the two full-SVD configurations have similar runtimes of 4.30 4.30 and 4.55 4.55 s per iteration. Matrix-free operators eliminate the need to materialize G res G_{\mathrm{res}} , reducing additional workspace from 𝒪 ⁡ ( d min ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(d_{\min}d) to 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( N + d ) ​ q ) \mathcal{O}((N+d)q) , excluding cached activations, output gradients, and projection bases. After training, both branches merge into the pre-trained weights, introducing no additional inference overhead.

We evaluate DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks: the 19 image classification tasks in VTAB-1K; object detection and instance segmentation on MS COCO; open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation (OVDG-SS) in both real-to-real and synthetic-to-real settings; eight commonsense reasoning tasks using LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B; and GLUE using DeBERTaV3-base. With τ = 5 \tau=5 , it requires 0.89 0.89 s per iteration, only 70 70 ms more than LoRA, and is 5.11 × 5.11\times faster than explicitly forming the residual gradient and applying full SVD ( 4.55 4.55 s per iteration). 2610.22438:64cc312345a2e3186d4540ac76d31.question: Across the 13 language-model fine-tuning pairs, how are stable rank and direction-count rank defined and compared with shape-matched random updates? What evidence links either measure to actual low-rank approximation error or retained model quality, and which controls support the interpretation?

passages.text: Studies of what fine-tuning does to a language model often summarise the weight update Δ ​ W \Delta W by its rank. We compare the rank measures used for this against the same measures on a random matrix of the same shape, and against two harder references: the pretrained weights, and matched fine-tunes without alignment content. Measures that count directions put our fine-tuning updates only a little below noise; stable rank, computed from the same singular values, puts them far below. Both are right: an update has a few strong directions on top of a long tail. The pattern holds for thirteen released pairs up to 8B parameters, and it is not a mark of alignment: with training held fixed, instruction data does not stand out from Wikipedia or code, DPO gives the same update whether its preference labels are real or half swapped at random (one model, modest preference strength), and scrambled text gives the most concentrated update of all. Applied to a recent claim that post-training is superficial because the effective rank of the weights barely changes, the baselines show that a random update of the same size leaves that rank almost unchanged while wrecking the model, and that an edit built on the effective rank of the update has no measurable effect in our tests. Rank measures of weight updates need a noise baseline, and claims about alignment need a control without alignment content.

When a language model is fine-tuned, each weight matrix W W changes by an update Δ ​ W \Delta W . 1 1 1 Large language model tools were used to assist with editing the prose and with writing analysis code; all ideas, experiments, analyses and claims are the author’s own. A natural way to ask what fine-tuning did is to ask how many independent directions Δ ​ W \Delta W uses, that is, its rank. A low-rank update suggests a small, targeted change; a full-rank one suggests a diffuse change. The question matters most for alignment. The superficial alignment hypothesis ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) holds that alignment mostly teaches a model which style to answer in, and output-level evidence supports it ( Lin et al., 2024 ) . If that is true, one might expect alignment to leave a small, structured footprint in the weights, and recent work has looked for one in the rank of Δ ​ W \Delta W and of W W ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . Related work reports that fine-tuning updates are “high rank” ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) or “nearly full-rank” ( Mukherjee et al., 2025 ) .

Real updates are full rank in the strict sense, so these readings rest on softer measures: the numerical rank, the number of directions that hold 90% of the energy ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) , or the entropy effective rank ( Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . Biderman et al. (2024) also compared against noise: the spectrum of a fully fine-tuned weight matrix looks like that of the pretrained one plus low-magnitude Gaussian noise, and they concluded that nothing about it is unusual. We began this project with the same impression. Counting the singular values of a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) update above 1% of the largest gave 97% of full rank, and the difference between two random initialisations of the same model, which is pure noise, gave 99.6%. By that measure, fine-tuning looks almost like noise. It is not. Stable rank ( Rudelson and Vershynin, 2007 ) , computed from the same singular values, puts the update 4.5 times below noise, and its top direction holds 6.6 times as much of the energy (4.2% against 0.6%). The two answers differ because the measures weigh different parts of the spectrum, and because measures of W W cannot see much of Δ ​ W \Delta W at all. Comparing against noise is an old idea in statistics ( Horn, 1965 ; Gavish and Donoho, 2014 ) , has been used to study trained weights ( Martin and Mahoney, 2021 ; Thamm et al., 2022 ) , and has been applied to fine-tuning updates before: Ryu et al. (2023) plot the spectrum of an update against a Marchenko–Pastur reference, and Biderman et al. (2024) against Gaussian noise. What has not been done is to apply it measure by measure, which is where the disagreement is, with matched controls for what the update was trained on. That is what this paper does. Our findings:

1. Counting measures compress the gap to noise. On our SFT, Wikipedia, code and direct preference optimisation (DPO) fine-tunes, the threshold count is only 2–5% below a random matrix of the same shape, and eRank and the 90% energy rank are 12–35% below it; stable rank is 78–94% below. Along the whole family of Rényi ranks the gap grows with how much weight a measure gives to the top directions, then levels off, as it must for any spectrum with a heavier head than noise; the point is how large the disagreement is (§ 4.1 ). 2. Updates have a few strong directions and a long tail , and on average are more concentrated than the pretrained weights they are added to (§ 4.2 ). 3. The shape does not single out alignment training. With the amount of training held fixed, the data does shape an update (code is the least concentrated, the more so with more training), but instruction SFT does not stand out from Wikipedia or Python code. DPO gives the same shape, and the same directions, whether it learns real preferences or randomly swapped ones that teach nothing. Text with its word order scrambled gives the most concentrated update of all (§ 4.3 ). 4. It holds for released models , thirteen base/instruct, post-training-stage and base/specialist pairs up to 8B parameters. On three bf16 updates (Qwen2.5-1.5B and the OLMo 2 DPO and RL stages), much of what the threshold count counts may be rounding (§ 4.4 ).

For each measure we report 1 − x ¯ update / x ¯ noise 1-\bar{x}_{\text{update}}/\bar{x}_{\text{noise}} , where x ¯ \bar{x} is the mean of the measure over all matrices of a model, whatever their shape: 0 means the update looks like noise, and values near 1 mean it is far more concentrated. (The noise value itself depends on the shape, from 0.25 to 0.53 for stable rank, Table 10 ; Table 11 gives the values by matrix type.) Intervals come from a bootstrap over layers (§ 3 ), and ratios quoted in the text, such as “4.5 times below noise”, use the unrounded means. The measures have different ceilings (the threshold count of noise is already 0.996), so the gap is best compared across updates for one measure, and only roughly across measures.

Rank measures that count directions describe fine-tuning updates as nearly full rank and put them only a little below random matrices of the same shape. Measures that weigh the top directions show the same updates to be far more concentrated than noise, and more concentrated than the pretrained weights. Both are right: the updates have a few strong directions and a long tail that holds most of the energy. With the amount of training held fixed, the data shapes an update somewhat, but instruction tuning does not stand out from Wikipedia or code; DPO gives the same shape and directions with real or half-swapped preferences; and scrambled text gives the most concentrated update. The shape is a property of fine-tuning, not a mark of alignment. An unchanged effective rank of the weights after post-training is what a random update of the same size also produces, and an edit built on the effective rank of the update does nothing measurable on two benchmarks. Our recommendation is simple: report any rank measure of a weight update next to its value on a random matrix of the same shape, check that low-precision training or storage did not erase the update, check that the two checkpoints are really related, and test claims about alignment against a fine-tune without alignment content.

2610.19761:6e154a1a3b650e027d511cf2c8f14.question: For the 19.08B MoE FineWeb pretraining run, which nine gradient-processing baselines were compared with CAST, how were learning rates and clipping settings tuned, and were training tokens, hardware, and compute matched? What are the validation-loss, throughput, and memory results?

passages.text: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW’s previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output’s estimated spectral norm sets each matrix’s threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline’s final smoothed training loss in 7.2% fewer steps.

A clipping threshold is meaningful only relative to the gradient scale. Persistent differences in row and column magnitudes affect the spectrum on which clipping acts. An unusually large value in one part of a matrix may be routine in another, and the overall scale can change over training. A fixed threshold may therefore apply different clipping strengths as the gradient scale changes. SPECTRA’s decaying pre-clipping threshold shows the value of adjusting this threshold during training. Such a schedule depends on the training step. A history-based rule can instead respond to changes in each matrix. We therefore use each matrix’s history to set its gradient scale and clipping threshold. 1. Output feedback τ = 1.3 ​ h old \tau=1.3h_{\rm old} V V next step Figure 2: CAST adds historical scaling (HS) and output feedback around SSC (Algorithm 1 ). AdamW uses restored G out G_{\rm out} ; its V V becomes the next V old V_{\rm old} , bias-corrected within S S . The EMA h old h_{\rm old} tracks the estimated ‖ Z out ‖ 2 \|Z_{\rm out}\|_{2} . Dashed histories advance only after a successful update. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), which uses two complementary histories (Figure 2 ). Historical scaling (HS) uses row and column summaries of AdamW’s previous second moment to set the scale for each gradient matrix. SSC acts in these standardized coordinates, and the output returns to its original scale before updating AdamW. AdamW updates both moments from this restored gradient. The updated second moment supplies the scale used at the next step.

We also maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) of the clipped output’s estimated spectral norm, computed in the same standardized coordinates. This estimate measures the largest singular value after clipping. The previous EMA sets the current threshold before clipping begins. CAST retains SSC’s soft map and Newton–Schulz routine. The two histories control the input coordinates and clipping threshold. Our contributions are threefold: • Historical scaling. We use row and column summaries of the previous second moment to define the coordinates of spectral clipping. We then restore the gradient’s original scale. • Output feedback. We adapt each matrix’s threshold to its clipped output history, so the threshold follows changes in the clipped spectrum. • Pretraining results. CAST achieves the lowest training and mean validation losses among nine baselines in our MoE study (Figure 1 ). We examine its component effects, gradient dynamics, and training cost.

CAST achieved the lowest training and mean validation losses among the nine baselines at step 5000 (Table 1 ). CAST’s mean validation loss was 1.26 × 10 − 2 1.26\times 10^{-2} below SSC-constant and 2.10 × 10 − 2 2.10\times 10^{-2} below SSC-cosine. CAST had lower loss on 20 and 19 subsets, respectively. SSC-cosine had higher training and mean validation losses than SSC-constant. AGC had the closest mean validation loss, with a gap of 1.18 × 10 − 2 1.18\times 10^{-2} . CAST’s training loss remained lowest across the 100-, 200-, and 500-step tail windows. Figure 4 shows the loss curves. Appendix D reports the losses for all 20 validation subsets. Figure 6: Raw input-gradient norms over iterations 501–5000 for ten primary conditions and three CAST ablations. CAST takes 2.0% longer per step than SSC-constant and 1.9% longer than ClipByValue. Timings include execution and logging and vary with cluster load. AdaGC has the lowest final smoothed loss among the baselines. CAST first reaches this loss at step 4,639, using 7.2% fewer steps (Figure 7 ). CAST uses two histories to guide spectral clipping in pretraining. AdamW’s previous second moment sets the gradient scale. An EMA of the clipped output’s estimated spectral norm sets each matrix’s threshold. In 5,000-step MoE pretraining, CAST achieved lower training and mean validation losses than nine baselines and three component variants. It also had the fewest relative gradient spikes. CAST reached AdaGC’s final smoothed loss in 7.2% fewer steps. Including per-step overhead, the estimated time saving is 5.5% relative to 5,000 ClipByValue steps. These results support using both histories to improve pretraining quality and efficiency.

Optimization algorithms can favor different solutions even when minimizing the same training objective, a phenomenon known as implicit bias ( Neyshabur et al., 2014 ; Gunasekar et al., 2017 ) . A classical example arises in linear classification with separable data, where logistic and exponential losses can approach zero only as the parameter norm diverges. In this setting, the limiting direction of the parameters becomes the object of interest. Gradient descent converges in direction to the Euclidean max-margin classifier ( Soudry et al., 2018 ; Nacson et al., 2019a ; Ji et al., 2020 ; Ji and Telgarsky, 2021 ) , whereas steepest descent under different norms can select different max-margin solutions ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Muon, an optimizer that has attracted considerable attention for large language model training ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , orthogonalizes matrix-valued updates rather than following conventional gradient directions. Ignoring momentum for simplicity, its idealized update maps a gradient matrix G = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ G=U\Sigma V^{\top} to its polar factor U ​ V ⊤ UV^{\top} . This update corresponds to steepest descent under the spectral norm, in contrast to the Frobenius-norm geometry of standard gradient descent. Recent work has studied the implicit bias of Muon with exact orthogonalization, establishing spectral max-margin behavior in linear multiclass classification ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) and margin stationarity in homogeneous neural networks ( Gronich and Vardi, 2026 ) .

However, these analyses rely on exact orthogonalization, which can be computationally expensive for large matrices. Practical Muon instead approximates the polar factor using a fixed number of Newton–Schulz iterations. Specifically, the original Muon optimizer proposed by Jordan et al. (2024) , when considered without momentum, normalizes the gradient as G / ( ∥ G ∥ F + ε ) G/(\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}+\varepsilon) , with a fixed stabilization constant ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , and then applies five Newton-Schulz iterations using a quintic polynomial. Whether these practical modifications preserve the spectral max-margin bias of idealized Muon remains unclear. This raises the central question of this work: Does practical Muon retain the spectral max-margin bias of its idealized counterpart? We show that the answer is negative: practical Muon with a fixed number of Newton-Schulz iterations and positive stabilization selects the Frobenius rather than the spectral max-margin direction on linear classification problems. The key technical idea is to express the practical Muon update as a gradient descent step plus a summable perturbation, thereby establishing that their parameter trajectories remain at bounded distance. We further investigate how the Newton–Schulz iteration count, stabilization constant, and polynomial choice affect the implicit bias and establish conditions under which spectral max-margin behavior can be recovered. Our contributions are as follows.

• We establish that Muon with a fixed number of Newton-Schulz iterations and positive stabilization leads to Frobenius max-margin selection on linear classification problems. Our results cover a general class of Newton–Schulz polynomials, including the quintic polynomial used in practical Muon, and extend to both exponential moving average and Nesterov-style momentum ( Section 3 ). • We examine how the Newton–Schulz iteration count, stabilization constant, and polynomial choice affect implicit bias. We show that removing stabilization alone does not necessarily restore spectral max-margin behavior: a fixed number of Newton-Schulz iterations can select directions that achieve neither Frobenius nor spectral max-margin. We further characterize the limiting behavior as the Newton–Schulz iteration count tends to infinity, revealing distinct asymptotic behaviors for the cubic and quintic polynomials ( Section 4.1 ). • We show that spectral max-margin behavior can be recovered with logarithmically growing Newton-Schulz iteration counts during training. For the cubic polynomial, this holds with a fixed positive stabilization constant, while for the quintic polynomial, we establish a recovery guarantee using gradient-dependent stabilization ( Section 4.2 ).

Kelner et al. (2014) develop a non-Euclidean generalization of gradient descent under arbitrary norms and apply it to approximate maximum-flow problems. In neural-network optimization, Carlson et al. (2015a) introduce stochastic spectral descent for restricted Boltzmann machines, using the spectral norm to exploit the matrix structure of the objective. Carlson et al. (2015b) combine non-Euclidean descent with preconditioning and study restricted Boltzmann machines, feedforward networks, and convolutional networks. Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) interpret several modern optimizers through steepest descent under parameter-dependent norms, including operator norms for matrix weights. Muon uses a small number of Newton–Schulz iterations to approximate orthogonalized momentum updates and has been applied to language-model and image-classification training ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . Liu et al. (2025) scale Muon to large language models through weight decay, update scaling, and distributed computation. Polynomial iterations have also been optimized for fast polar approximation in Muon ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . Kim and Oh (2026) establish convergence guarantees for Muon with Newton–Schulz iterations, whereas de Oliveira et al. (2026) analyze a soft-sign surrogate. Li and Tsuchiya (2026) investigate the smoothing effects of finite Newton–Schulz iterations in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, while Peng et al. (2026) analyze convergence of practical Muon with finite Newton–Schulz iterations and Nesterov-style momentum. Unlike these convergence analyses, our work focuses on how the Newton–Schulz iteration count, stabilization constant, and polynomial choice determine the asymptotic max-margin behavior.

This paper establishes that Muon with finite Newton–Schulz iterations and positive stabilization selects the Frobenius max-margin direction in separable linear classification. We also characterize the effects of stabilization, iteration count, and polynomial choice, and provide conditions for recovering spectral max-margin behavior. Our results focus on full-batch linear classification, leaving stochastic optimization and nonlinear neural networks beyond the present analysis. Motivated by the asymptotic connection to gradient descent in linear classification, an interesting direction for future work is to investigate whether similar behavior emerges in later stages of large-scale neural network training.

2610.19844:69652762966bb798b831fe96269a8.question: In LLM pretraining, what validation loss or perplexity, peak training memory, and step time does SMRC or its Muon variant achieve versus GaLore, full-space Muon, and other subspace optimizers at matched model, rank, data, and token budget?

passages.text: We adopt the LLaMA architecture ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) and train models with 60 60 M, 150 150 M, 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B parameters. Their architectural configurations are summarized in Table 4 . All models are pretrained on the C4 dataset ( Raffel et al., 2020 ) .

Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

In this paper, we investigate memory-efficient subspace optimization and adopt a residual correction framework. For momentum SGD, our proposed SMRC combines projected momentum with a gradient correction in the orthogonal complement and achieves an O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) convergence rate, which matches that of full-space momentum SGD. We generalize SMRC to a multi-stage variant with arbitrary basis refreshes and introduce a boundary correction that aligns consecutive virtual iterates, while retaining a convergence rate of the same order as the single-stage method. Furthermore, we extend this framework to Muon and propose PMRC, which achieves an O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) rate under a mixed stationarity measure, while the multi-stage variant retains a convergence rate of the same order. The convergence rates of both PMRC variants are of the same order as that of full-space Muon. Both SMRC and PMRC reduce the optimizer-state memory from O ⁡ ( m ​ n ) O(mn) to O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . Extensive experimental results on LLM pretraining and supervised finetuning tasks demonstrate the practical effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed methods.

For all ablations, we pretrain LLaMA-150M on the C4 dataset for 9900 9900 steps with a sequence length of 512 512 and a global batch size of 512 512 . We refresh the projection basis every 100 100 steps and, unless otherwise stated, set the residual cap to ρ = 4 \rho=4 . Effect of the subspace rank. We vary the projection rank over r ∈ { 64,128,256,512 } r\in\{64,128,256,512\} with the residual weight fixed at γ = 8192 \gamma=8192 and all other settings unchanged. Increasing r r expands the subspace in which momentum is maintained and the matrix-sign transformation is applied. As shown in Figure 3 , a larger rank reduces the validation loss, but also increases the memory required to store the projection basis and the projected momentum. For a parameter matrix of size m × n m\times n , this memory cost scales as O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . These results illustrate the trade-off between validation performance and optimizer-state memory when choosing the subspace rank. Effect of the residual weight. We fix the rank at r = 256 r=256 and vary the residual weight over γ ∈ { 0 , 1024 , 2048 , 4096 , 8192 } \gamma\in\{0,1024,2048,4096,8192\} with all other settings unchanged. Since the residual cap remains active, γ \gamma serves as an upper bound on the effective weight applied to each parameter matrix rather than its exact value. As shown in Figure 4 , the validation loss decreases monotonically as γ \gamma increases over the tested range, with diminishing improvements at larger values. In particular, γ = 0 \gamma=0 removes the residual correction and yields the highest validation loss. This comparison supports the benefit of incorporating gradient information from the orthogonal complement in LLM pretraining. Figure 5: Effect of the residual cap on PMRC.

Effect of the residual cap. We finally examine the role of the residual cap in stabilizing training. Under the practical update in Eq. ( 32 ), the effective residual weight is γ ^ k , t = min ⁡ { γ , ρ ​ ∥ P k ​ Z k , t ∥ F 2 max ⁡ { ∥ R k , t ∥ F 2 , ϵ } } . \widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}=\min\left\{\gamma,\rho\sqrt{\frac{\lVert P_{k}Z_{k,t}\rVert_{F}^{2}}{\max\{\lVert R_{k,t}\rVert_{F}^{2},\epsilon\}}}\right\}. By construction, this rule ensures ∥ γ ^ k , t ​ R k , t ∥ F ≤ ρ ​ ∥ P k ​ Z k , t ∥ F \lVert\widehat{\gamma}_{k,t}R_{k,t}\rVert_{F}\leq\rho\lVert P_{k}Z_{k,t}\rVert_{F} . We compare the default choice ρ = 4 \rho=4 with an uncapped run, fixing r = 256 r=256 and γ = 8192 \gamma=8192 in both runs. Without the cap, the full residual gradient is multiplied by γ \gamma at every step. As shown in Figure 5 , the uncapped run becomes unstable during early training. This observation supports the use of the residual cap to control excessively large residual updates, while retaining the original coefficient γ \gamma whenever the correction is below the threshold.

One-shot pruning and low-rank decompositions for LLMs. Post-training one-shot compression is a training-free paradigm popularized by SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) , which compresses a pretrained LLM layer-by-layer on a small calibration set by minimizing the layerwise reconstruction error ‖ 𝐗𝐖 − 𝐗 ​ 𝐖 ^ ‖ F 2 \|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2} subject to a structural constraint on 𝐖 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{W}} ; methods differ along two axes: the constraint family and the per-layer solver. Pure sparsity : SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) uses a sequential column-based sparsification scheme: after sparsifying one column, the remaining weights are updated to compensate for the incurred error, while ALPS ( Meng et al., 2024 ) formulates the same problem as a constrained quadratic problem solved by the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) ( Boyd et al., 2011 ) . Pure low-rank : SVD-LLM(W) ( Wang et al., 2025 ) uses a whitened Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to minimize layerwise reconstruction error; ASVD ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) instead scales input channels using activation statistics before SVD. Sparse + low-rank ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) : OATS ( Zhang and Papyan, 2025 ) and Hassle-free ( Makni et al., 2025 ) alternate a sparse fitting step with a low-rank projection step; OATS scores weights using a per-row activation-norm criterion whereas Hassle-free uses the full input correlation matrix. 3BASiL ( Makni et al., 2026 ) runs a multi-block ADMM that jointly minimizes the sparse and low-rank components simultaneously. Our method CACTUS differs from all these layerwise reconstruction algorithms by incorporating downstream gradients in its objective, making it curvature-aware rather than gradient-blind .

ultaneously. Our method CACTUS differs from all these layerwise reconstruction algorithms by incorporating downstream gradients in its objective, making it curvature-aware rather than gradient-blind . This is best illustrated in Figure 1 .

In this paper, we first highlight the connection between downstream utility and influence preservation through the curvature-aware objective introduced in Equation 1 . Our new algorithm CACTUS makes optimizing this objective practical for modern LLM pruning as well as ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) decomposition tasks. It runs at a substantially lower cost compared to prior state-of-the-art curvature-aware pruning methods. Across various compression settings, model architectures, and gradient projection strategies, CACTUS consistently improves downstream utility while retaining gradient fidelity. Limitations. In this paper, we focus on pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) compression. Extending our ADMM framework to quantization and mixed quantization-sparsity settings are directions for future work, especially when reparameterizations (e.g., rotations) change gradient geometry. We also only consider uniform compression budgets; it would be interesting to design specialized methods that can allocate sparsity and rank non-uniformly across the entire LLM layers. Additionally, we do not study post-compression refinements like full-model or LoRA-style finetuning. These may trade off deployment quality and gradient alignment fidelity in different ways. We leave these interesting follow-up research directions for future work.

All one-shot baselines are run in the same layerwise compression framework and with the same calibration samples, except when a method explicitly includes a post-compression stage. SparseGPT , ALPS , SVD-LLM(W) (simple activation-aware low-rank fitting without sequential factor refinement or post-compression fine-tuning), OATS , and 3BASiL use activation-only objectives using 𝐇 \mathbf{H} , whereas IPSVD , IProX , LLM-Surgeon , and CACTUS use 𝐆 \mathbf{G} as well. For ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) baselines at target compression ratio c c , we match total parameter budget using the same layerwise rank allocation r ℓ = ⌊ η ⁡ ( 1 − c ) ​ m ℓ ​ n ℓ / ( m ℓ + n ℓ ) ⌋ r_{\ell}=\lfloor\eta(1-c)m_{\ell}n_{\ell}/(m_{\ell}+n_{\ell})\rfloor with η = 0.3 \eta=0.3 ; for named structured settings such as ( 2 : 4 + r ​ 256 ) (2{:}4{+}r256) , the sparsity pattern and rank are fixed exactly as specified. For LLM-Surgeon, we use row-wise correlated weight updates ( max_correlate=-1 ), jointly accounting for the pruned weights within each row when computing weight compensation, for both unstructured and 2:4 pruning. We also employ the five-shot setting described in Section 3.1 , since the one-shot unstructured pruning on Llama3.2-1B produced weak results. For Qwen3-4B model under 2:4 sparsity on MLP layers, one-shot results are competitive, so we report both one-shot and five-shot results.
